```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys, pathlib
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path.cwd() / "src"))
from lectures import plotting, datasets
from lectures.plotting import INK, COOL, WARM, CRASH, despine, annotate_box
from rbig import AnnealedRBIG
from lectures.measures import cocrash_fraction
plotting.set_style("notes")
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

To carry uncertainty forward you must **sample**.  This page climbs the ladder of
ways to sample a *joint* distribution — and shows that only the ones built on
[Gaussianization](../gaussianization/index.qmd) keep the co-crash that risk cares
about.

## Rung 1 · Independent Sampling — Fails

The obvious move is to sample each variable from its own (correct) marginal.  It
gets every marginal right and the **joint catastrophically wrong**: independence
*by construction* can never produce the co-crash.

```{python}
#| label: fig-independent-fail
#| fig-cap: "Real co-crashing pair, independent resampling (co-crash destroyed), and RBIG samples (co-crash restored). Shaded = joint lower-tail."
a, b = datasets.tail_dependent_pair(n=2000, seed=0)
X = np.column_stack([a, b])
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
indep = np.column_stack([rng.permutation(a), rng.permutation(b)])
gen = AnnealedRBIG(n_layers=30, random_state=0).fit(X).sample(2000)

panels = [(X, COOL, "real"), (indep, CRASH, "independent resample"),
          (gen, plotting.PALETTE["green"], "RBIG backward")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4.4))
for ax, (data, col, name) in zip(axes, panels):
    cc = cocrash_fraction(data[:, 0], data[:, 1])
    ax.scatter(data[:, 0], data[:, 1], s=7, c=col, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
    ax.axvspan(-6, np.quantile(data[:, 0], 0.1), color=CRASH, alpha=0.06)
    ax.axhspan(-6, np.quantile(data[:, 1], 0.1), color=CRASH, alpha=0.06)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nco-crash = {cc:.0%}", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xlim(-5, 4); ax.set_ylim(-5, 4)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The marginals are identical in all three panels.  Independence throws away the
one thing the portfolio fears.

## Rung 2 · Gaussian Monte-Carlo — Right Correlation, Wrong Extremes

Fit a covariance, sample a multivariate normal.  Cheap, and it captures linear
co-movement — but Gaussian tails are **thin**, so it understates the worst joint
losses.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why Gaussian Tails Are Thin, Precisely
A Gaussian density decays like $e^{-x^2/2}$; a Student-$t$ decays only
polynomially, $\sim |x|^{-(\nu+1)}$.  Worse, a Gaussian copula has *asymptotic
tail independence* — the probability both assets breach an extreme quantile
together $\to 0$ as the quantile deepens, however high the correlation.  Matching
the covariance is not matching the tail.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-gauss-mc
#| fig-cap: "Real (tail-dependent) returns vs a Gaussian Monte-Carlo with the same covariance. Same bulk; the portfolio-loss tail and 1% VaR are understated by the Gaussian."
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n = 4000
z = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
a2 = 0.5 * z + 0.5 * rng.normal(0, 1, n)
b2 = 0.5 * z + 0.5 * rng.normal(0, 1, n)
crash = rng.random(n) < 0.05
shock = np.abs(rng.standard_t(2.5, n) * 3.0)
a2 = np.where(crash, a2 - shock, a2)
b2 = np.where(crash, b2 - shock, b2)
D = np.column_stack([a2, b2]); D = (D - D.mean(0)) / D.std(0)
gmc = rng.multivariate_normal(D.mean(0), np.cov(D.T), size=n)

port_real, port_gmc = D[:, 0] + D[:, 1], gmc[:, 0] + gmc[:, 1]
var_real, var_gmc = np.quantile(port_real, 0.01), np.quantile(port_gmc, 0.01)

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.4))
axL.scatter(D[:, 0], D[:, 1], s=7, c=COOL, alpha=0.25, edgecolors="none", label="real")
axL.scatter(gmc[:, 0], gmc[:, 1], s=7, c=CRASH, alpha=0.2, edgecolors="none",
            label="Gaussian MC")
axL.set_xlim(-8, 4); axL.set_ylim(-8, 4)
axL.set_title("real vs Gaussian MC", fontsize=12)
axL.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, markerscale=2)
axL.set_xticks([]); axL.set_yticks([]); despine(axL)

bins = np.linspace(min(port_real.min(), port_gmc.min()), 3, 60)
axR.hist(port_real, bins=bins, density=True, color=COOL, alpha=0.55, label="real")
axR.hist(port_gmc, bins=bins, density=True, color=CRASH, alpha=0.45, label="Gaussian MC")
axR.axvline(var_real, color=COOL, lw=2, ls="--")
axR.axvline(var_gmc, color=CRASH, lw=2, ls="--")
axR.set_title("portfolio loss & 1% VaR", fontsize=12)
annotate_box(axR, 0.5, -0.12,
             f"1% VaR:  real {var_real:.1f}   vs   Gaussian {var_gmc:.1f}")
axR.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False); despine(axR)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The Gaussian draws the same cloud in the middle but **misses the co-extremes** —
its VaR is too optimistic by a wide margin.

## Rung 3 · RBIG Backward — The Hero

Learn $T$ with RBIG, sample in the Gaussian space, invert.  The generated
scenarios keep the **real** joint tail: the same tool that *measured* dependence
in Chapter 1, now a *generator*.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rbig-scenarios
#| fig-cap: "Real returns and RBIG-generated scenarios: the lower-tail co-crash matches."
gen2 = AnnealedRBIG(n_layers=30, random_state=0).fit(D).sample(n)
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, data, col, name in [
    (axL, D, COOL, f"real · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(D[:,0], D[:,1], 0.05):.0%}"),
    (axR, gen2, plotting.PALETTE["green"],
     f"RBIG scenarios · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(gen2[:,0], gen2[:,1], 0.05):.0%}"),
]:
    ax.scatter(data[:, 0], data[:, 1], s=7, c=col, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_xlim(-8, 4); ax.set_ylim(-8, 4)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.eli5}
**One-liner recap.**  Independent sampling kills the joint; Gaussian Monte-Carlo
keeps the correlation but thins the tail; RBIG (or a flow) run backward keeps the
*real* joint extremes — the only honest scenario generator of the three.
:::
